questions.q: Why does this lesson's producer set both acks=all and enable.idempotence?
options: acks=all confirms every in-sync replica has the write; enable.idempotence stops the producer's own retry from writing that same event twice
The two settings do exactly the same thing, so either one alone would be enough
acks=all disables replication entirely to speed up writes
enable.idempotence removes the need for any replication at all
questions.explain: acks=all is Lesson 11's replication guarantee turned on; enable.idempotence closes the duplicate-write gap that a lost acknowledgment can otherwise open.

questions.q: Why does the orders topic get exactly 6 partitions, according to this lesson?
options: So the consumer group can scale to 6 active members before any consumer sits idle
6 is Kafka's hard-coded default partition count for every topic
Because 6 partitions is the maximum Kafka allows on a single topic
Partition count has no relationship to how many consumers a group can usefully have
questions.explain: A consumer group can only have as many active members as there are partitions on the topic it's reading — sizing for 6 partitions means the group can scale to 6 members.

questions.q: What does setting enable.auto.commit=False and committing manually, after processing, actually buy this consumer group?
options: The worst case on a crash is re-processing an already-handled event, never silently losing one
It guarantees exactly-once processing with zero duplicates, ever
It removes the need for a consumer group entirely
It makes the consumer read faster by skipping offset tracking altogether
questions.explain: Auto-commit on a timer can advance the offset before processing finishes; committing manually after process_order() succeeds means a crash can only cause a re-process, not a silent loss.

questions.q: Why does the orders topic get 7 days of retention (604800000 ms) in this lesson's example, specifically?
options: So there's a genuinely usable replay window if a downstream job needs to reprocess before the data ages out
7 days is the shortest retention period Kafka technically allows
Retention has no effect on what a consumer can replay
Longer retention makes the producer write faster
questions.explain: Retention (Lesson 13) sets how far back a consumer can replay from — 7 days gives real room to catch and reprocess before the events are gone.

questions.q: What is this lesson's actual point, given that Lessons 6 through 9 already covered producers, consumers, consumer groups, and delivery semantics individually?
options: Showing how those separate ideas compose into one real, deliberately-configured pipeline, not introducing new concepts
Replacing everything taught in Lessons 6 through 9 with a completely different approach
Introducing a brand-new Kafka API that hasn't been covered before
Proving that consumer groups are unnecessary for a real pipeline
questions.explain: Every setting in this lesson's producer, topic, and consumer group was already introduced earlier — what's new is seeing them chosen together for one working pipeline.
